newsitem.title: UK: IBCA rates Kazakhstan BB minus foriegn currency.
newsitem.headline: IBCA rates Kazakhstan BB minus foriegn currency.

text.p: IBCA, the European credit rating agency, said on Tuesday it assigned the Republic of Kazakhstan a long-term foreign currency rating of BB minus.
"The rating will apply to the forthcoming debut eurobond issue of the republic and will act as a ceiling for IBCA's ratings of Kazakh banks and corporates," IBCA said in a statement.
At the same time, IBCA assigned a short-term foreign currency rating of B for obligations with a maturity of less than one year.

"Kazakhstan's potential as an oil and gas producer, with reserves nearly as large as those of Kuwait, is enormous but its landlocked position in central Asia continues to make it reliant on Russia and other neighbours for access to western markets," IBCA said. "The planned pipeline to the Black Sea, now agreed with Russia, will increase exports by half over the next two years. Kazakhstan also benefits from considerable mineral wealth where transport constraints are less."

"The lack of a track record as an independent state - with all that this implies for the inexperience of the national bureaucracy in forming and implementing policy - is a key constraint on the rating," IBCA said.

The rating agency particularly pointed out the problems that Kazakhstan suffered in maintaining timely debt service of sovereign-guaranteed debts incurred since independence (All previous debt was assumed by the Russian Federation).
IBCA said the recent Russian decision to cut off the electricity in northern and eastern Kazakhstan underlines the dependence of the Kazakh economy on its northern neighbour.

"With a substantial Russian minority of almost the same size as the Kazakh minority - 37 percent of the 16.5 million population, against 43 percent - Russia is likely to continue to exercise enormous influence over a state that had not sought independence from the Soviet Union," IBCA said. "Kazakhstan can show considerable progress in reducing inflation, and fiscal policy has also been run on very tight lines, with the burden of any shortfall in tax revenues coming immediately onto public spending," IBCA said. "There is also a consensus on macroeconomic stability, which will contribute to further GDP growth next year."

"However, economic restructuring has been slow and uncertain," the rating agency said. "Although there has been progress in privatising small and medium sized companies, the big enterprises which account for the bulk of GDP remain in the state sector so that Kazakhstan's private sector share of GDP is little more than 40 percent, even if foreign managed companies still majority owned by the state are included."
